title: Press Release
first_summary: Domestic demand drives a robust economic expansion in Bulgaria, though inflation remains elevated. GDP grew by 3.4 percent in 2024 and 3.2 percent in the first half of 2025, with growth projected at around 3 percent in 2025 and 2026. Headline inflation is projected to average around 3½ percent in 2025 and 2026. Staff recommend tighter fiscal policy, moderating public wage growth, removing the cap on insurable income, increasing tax rates, and managing credit market risks through macroprudential policy.

title: Key Issues
first_summary: Euro area accession in January 2026 provides a near-term boost to the outlook and raises medium-term growth. Supporting this outlook, GDP growth is projected to be strong at around 3 percent in 2025 and 2026. IMF staff recommend tighter fiscal policy, noting a neutral fiscal stance requires an adjustment of about 1 percent of GDP. Staff also recommend moderating public wage growth, maintaining nimble macroprudential policy, and pursuing structural, governance, and energy sector reforms.

title: Context
first_summary: Bulgaria approaches euro adoption in January 2026 as an opportunity to raise medium-term growth, though fiscal, inflationary, and competitiveness pressures are emerging. Real income convergence has accelerated, but unit labor costs are outstripping productivity growth while credit expands rapidly. Policymaking is complicated by political fragmentation, with the October 2024 election marking the seventh vote in four years, despite the government approving the 2025 budget. Realizing the full benefits of euro adoption will depend on maintaining reform momentum and policy continuity.

title: Recent Economic Developments
first_summary: Domestic demand is driving a robust expansion. Real GDP grew by 3.4 percent in 2024 and by 3.2 percent in the first half of 2025, supported by real wage growth of about 9 percent. After closing 2024 at 2.1 percent, headline inflation rose to 3.4 percent in the first half of 2025, and core inflation reached 3 percent. Credit to the non-financial private sector grew by 14 percent (August, y-o-y), with mortgage loans at 30 percent. Staff recommended borrower-based measures consistent with October 2024 BNB actions.

title: Outlook And Risks
first_summary: The near-term growth outlook is positive, though risks are elevated and mostly tilted to the downside. Growth is projected to remain robust at around 3 percent in 2025 and 2026, while private credit is projected to keep growing at double digits in 2026. However, the current account is projected to weaken to -3.8 percent in 2025, and average inflation is expected to remain elevated at around 3½ percent in 2025 and 2026. Externally, a downside scenario could lower growth by 0.1–0.2 percentage points, on average per year, over 2025–30.

title: Policy Discussions
first_summary: Euro adoption provides an opportunity to strengthen institutions, enhance policy credibility, and raise medium-term growth. To fully realize these benefits and avoid macro-financial imbalances, IMF staff recommend tightening fiscal policy from short-term demand support towards investment and raising revenue via progressive income taxation. Policymakers should also monitor credit and liquidity risks to adjust macroprudential policies, and accelerate structural reforms in governance, energy, infrastructure, and human capital to raise productivity, benefit from the EU single market, and secure RRP disbursements.

title: A. Fiscal Policy to Anchor Macroeconomic Stability
first_summary: An expansionary fiscal stance is projected for 2025 and 2026, driven by higher spending and weaker revenues. Staff projects a fiscal impulse of 0.7 percent of GDP in 2025 and lower projected revenues of 2.7 percent of GDP in 2025. IMF staff project an overall balance of -3.4 percent of GDP in 2025 and -3.5 percent of GDP in 2026. Staff recommends a neutral stance needing an adjustment of about 1 percent of GDP relative to baseline projections, alongside moderating public wage growth and pension reforms.

title: B. Financial Policies to Minimize Risks
first_summary: The financial sector remains resilient, but rapid consumer and mortgage credit growth has heightened systemic risks in the real estate market. In support, banks maintain a CAR of 23 percent and a 2.3 percent return on assets, while housing loans grow at 27 percent y/y and house price growth reached 15.1 percent y/y in Q1 2025 with overvaluation of 10–15 percent. IMF staff recommend close monitoring of overvaluation, nimbly adjusting macroprudential instruments, and potentially tightening the DSTI limit of 50 percent if house price growth does not abate.

title: C. Structural Policies to Raise Medium-Term Growth
first_summary: Bulgaria faces growth headwinds from low productivity and a shrinking population, with the working-age population expected to decline by as much as 20 percent in the next 25 years. Closing half of structural policy gaps could raise GDP by 5–10 percent. Absorbing EU funds fully would boost GDP by 1 percent in 2030, or 2.3 percent with efficiency gains; however, only 22 percent (EUR 1.4 bn) of RRP grants were disbursed as of end-September 2025. Staff recommend implementing RRP reforms, investing in human capital, and improving governance.

title: Staff Appraisal
first_summary: Economic momentum is strong and inflation is elevated, while the external position in 2024 is assessed to be broadly in line with fundamentals, though fiscal policy is expected to remain expansionary in 2025–26. Staff recommend fiscal tightening in 2026 to cool the economy by achieving a neutral fiscal stance, removing the cap on insurable income, raising tax rates, and using borrower-based macroprudential measures. Staff also recommend holding the next Article IV consultation on the standard 12 - month cycle.

faults: The summary misattributes the removal of the cap on insurable income as a fiscal tightening measure by stating 'Staff recommend fiscal tightening in 2026 to cool the economy by ... removing the cap on insurable income', whereas the source discusses removing the cap in the context of pension reform.

The summary incorrectly bundles borrower-based macroprudential measures into the fiscal tightening recommendations with the phrase 'Staff recommend fiscal tightening in 2026 to cool the economy by ... using borrower-based macroprudential measures', whereas macroprudential policy is discussed separately from fiscal policy in the source.

For pension sustainability, staff advise removing the cap on insurable income. title: Selected Figures and Statistical Tables
first_summary: Bulgaria's economic growth was generally stronger than in peers in the last three years, driven by the services sector. Real GDP grew 3.4 percent in 2024, up from 1.7 percent in 2023. Real domestic demand increased 4.7 percent in 2024, supported by private consumption growth of 4.9 percent in 2024. Gross external debt remained stable at 47.6 percent of GDP in 2024, while general government gross debt was 23.8 percent of GDP in 2024. The text makes no staff recommendations.

title: Annex I. Risk Assessment Matrix
first_summary: Bulgaria faces significant domestic and global risks, including fiscal policy miscalibration, political instability, trade barriers, commodity price volatility, and geopolitical tensions. Supporting these assessments, low relative likelihood indicates a probability below 10 percent, medium is between 10 and 30 percent, and high is between 30 and 50 percent. Staff recommend tightening fiscal policy to support disinflation, shoring up political consensus on policy continuity, continuously monitoring credit risks, tightening macroprudential policies as needed, and deploying targeted, time-bound support for vulnerable groups during severe disruptions.

title: Annex II. External Sector Assessment
first_summary: The external position in 2024 is assessed to be broadly in line with the level implied by medium-term fundamentals and desirable policies. Supporting this, the NIIP reached -4.4 percent of GDP in 2024, while the current account declined to -1.6 percent of GDP in 2024 against a model norm of -1.5 percent of GDP in 2024. External debt stood at 47.6 percent of GDP in 2024. Staff recommend policies that stimulate investment, raise Bulgaria’s productivity and potential growth, foster economic convergence, and boost non-price competitive factors.

Staff recommend policies that stimulate investment, raise Bulgaria’s productivity and potential growth, foster economic convergence, and boost non-price competitive factors.

title: Annex III. Debt Sustainability Analysis
first_summary: Bulgaria faces a low overall risk of sovereign stress, with public debt sustainable and the second lowest in the EU. Public debt is projected to increase from 23.8 percent of GDP in 2024 to 38.5 percent of GDP in 2034, remaining below 60 percent of GDP by 2030 in fanchart simulations. The primary deficit is 2.5 percent of GDP in 2024. Over the longer run, Bulgaria should continue with reforms to tackle fiscal pressures from challenges such as ageing, defense, and energy transition.

title: Annex IV. Data Issues
first_summary: Data provided to the Fund are adequate for surveillance, although external sector statistics coverage and granularity assessments changed to "B" amid persistent and large balance of payments revisions. Supporting this, Bulgaria adheres to the Special Data Dissemination Standard (SDDS) Plus since May 2016, with indicators tracked as of September 30, 2025. Staff indicate that more information on budgetary government flows between budgetary central government and SOEs would help better identify and monitor fiscal risks.

title: Annex V. Past Fund Advice
first_summary: Policy actions on 2024 Article IV recommendations were partially implemented, achieving a neutral fiscal stance in 2024. Pre-pandemic VAT rates were fully restored as of January 2025, but no RRP installments were disbursed in 2024 and H1 2025. In October 2024, the BNB introduced an LTV limit of 85 percent, a DSTI limit of 50 percent, and a maturity limit of 30 years. Staff recommend moving from low 10 percent corporate and personal income tax rates to higher, progressive rates to raise revenue.

faults: The summary misattributes the IMF's policy advice as current staff recommendations by stating that "Staff recommend moving from low 10 percent corporate and personal income tax rates to higher, progressive rates to raise revenue" when the source actually lists this under past 2024 Article IV recommendations.

summary: Policy progress on 2024 Article IV recommendations was mixed. Pre-pandemic VAT rates were fully restored as of January 2025, but no RRP installments were disbursed in 2024 and H1 2025, leading to RRP renegotiation in 2025. In October 2024, the BNB introduced borrower-based measures, including an LTV limit of 85 percent, a DSTI limit of 50 percent, and a maturity limit of 30 years. Past 2024 advice recommended moving from 10 percent flat tax rates, but no reform was initiated, with a pension roadmap expected for end-2025.

title: Annex VI. Benefits and Challenges from Euro Adoption
first_summary: Bulgaria’s euro adoption in January 2026 offers key benefits like lower transaction costs alongside challenges from price conversion and excess bank liquidity. Figures show the one-time price level impact for early adopters was limited to between 0.1 and 0.3 percentage points, while domestic bank reserve requirements will drop by 11 percentage points to 1 percent of eligible liabilities in January 2026. Staff recommend using macroprudential policy to manage demand, including periodically reassessing October 2024 borrower-based measures currently set at 50 and 15 percent.

title: Informational Annex

Since January 1, 1999, the lev has been fixed at BGN 1.95583 per euro. Projected annual charges to the Fund are 0.01 SDR Million for 2025 through 2029. Staff offer no recommendations.

title: Staff Supplement
first_summary: The 2026 draft budget targets a deficit of 3 percent of GDP, but fiscal challenges persist as staff view revenue gains as optimistic. Revenue policy measures raise about 1.2 percent of GDP, while tax administration measures target about 1.4 percent of GDP. Spending includes an 11 percent wage increase and about 0.4 percent of GDP in discretionary spending. Public debt will increase to about 31 percent of GDP in 2026, including 2.6 percent of GDP in SAFE borrowing. Staff recommend social security contribution rate increases.

faults: Staff recommend social security contribution rate increases.

However, public wage expenditure will grow by about 11 percent, and public debt is projected to increase to about 31 percent of GDP in 2026.
